e.t: This word means “good” and functions as an adverb, describing an action or circumstance as being done or proceeding in a good way. Because it is an adverb, it modifies the manner or character of what is expressed in the sentence rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, in two separate verses. The surrounding verse determines precisely what it describes.

This adjective describes someone or something that is inflexible—firm, resistant to change, or not easily bent. It presents a quality of steadfast refusal rather than softness or adaptability. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, once in Sirach 30:8 and once in 4 Maccabees 15:13. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain what is described in each passage, but the basic meaning remains the same: unyielding or inflexible.

This noun refers to an unpleasant feeling or a sense of nausea. It describes something disagreeable or sickening rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 23:29. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be described further; its ordinary meaning remains the experience of unpleasantness or nauseousness.

This Greek word means “pain” or “suffering.” It is a noun describing distress or affliction endured by a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Psalms 38:3 and Ecclesiastes 1:18 and 2:23. These uses place the word within reflections on bodily or inward distress, while the precise force in each passage depends on its surrounding verse and context. Its central idea remains an experience of pain, hardship, or suffering rather than an action or person.

This Greek LXX verb means “form anew; remodel”: to reshape something or make it into a new form. As a verb, it describes an act of remaking rather than a finished object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 15:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is the deliberate reshaping or refashioning of something already existing.

This Greek LXX verb means “raise its feathers,” describing feathers being lifted or made to stand up. It names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus: once each in Proverbs 7:11, Sirach 34:1, and Song of Songs 6:5. The surrounding verse determines how this action functions in each passage, but its central meaning remains the raising of feathers.

Anemelech is a proper name, rendered as “Anēmelech” or “Animelekh.” It identifies a particular named figure or designation rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, the name occurs once, at 2 Kings 17:31. The reference identifies where the name appears, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific role in that passage.

This Greek adverb means “forthwith” or “without delay,” describing an action done immediately and without postponement. It answers the question of when something happens, emphasizing promptness rather than a gradual process. In the Greek text of 3 Maccabees, it occurs twice, both times in chapter 5. Its precise force in either sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary sense is clear: something happens at once or promptly.

This noun means “pear tree,” referring to the tree that bears pears. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 14:14–15. The word identifies a real kind of tree rather than expressing an abstract quality, action, or person. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a pear tree.

This Greek LXX noun means a “hiding place”—a concealed location where someone or something can be kept out of sight or sheltered. It presents the idea of concealment or refuge rather than an action. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX corpus, appearing in 2 Samuel, Job, and Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a place of hiding or concealment.

This verb means “destroy” or “lose.” It can describe something being ruined or brought to an end, or something becoming lost. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on destruction or loss. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 345 times, so it is a broadly used word rather than one limited to a single setting. Its range includes both the act of destroying and the result of being lost.

This Greek verb means to “pay off” or “repay”—to give back what is owed or required. It describes settling a debt, making restitution, or returning a due payment. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 28 times, especially in Exodus, where laws address repayment for harm, loss, or property. The word therefore focuses on restoring what another person is entitled to receive, rather than merely giving something voluntarily.

This word means “idleness” or “laziness”—a lack of purposeful work or activity. As a noun, it describes the condition or quality of being inactive rather than the act of working. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears five times, including one English rendering as “idleness.” Its references span Exodus, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Wisdom, and Sirach, showing that the word can describe an unproductive condition across different kinds of passages.

Arouēl, also given as Aroil, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 15:22. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the verse text or surrounding context, its specific referent cannot be described more precisely here. The name’s role is therefore to identify a particular biblical entity in that passage.

Aseroth, also rendered Asiroth, is a proper name identifying a particular named place in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs seven times in the LXX, chiefly in Numbers, with additional occurrences in Deuteronomy and 1 Chronicles. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains that of a geographic name preserved across these scriptural references.

Bakbouk, also rendered Vakvuk, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice: once in Ezra 2:51 and once in Nehemiah 7:53. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whom it identifies or what role that person has. Its meaning is therefore best given as the personal name “Bakbouk; Vakvuk.”

This noun means “profanation”: treating something holy as common, defiled, or unworthy of its sacred use. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it names the act or condition of violating the holiness attached to a person, place, object, or covenant-related matter. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, including uses in Leviticus and Numbers, and also in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the desecration of what is holy.

This word is a proper name referring to Bethasmoth, also rendered Vithazmoth. It functions as a place name rather than a description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:28, within the list of returned families and settlements. The word’s significance is therefore identifying a particular location; its precise setting belongs to the surrounding passage rather than to the name’s basic lexical function.

This Greek LXX noun means “ox,” referring to a large domesticated cattle animal. It is used as an ordinary name for the animal rather than as an abstract idea or action. The word occurs 140 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, showing that it is a regularly used term for livestock in biblical language. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and how the ox is being mentioned there.

This adverb means “slowly,” describing an action that proceeds without speed or haste. It tells how something happens rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:17. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a gradual or unhurried manner of action.

Gabriel is a proper name referring to the person called Gabriel. In the Greek Septuagint text, this name appears twice, both times in Daniel: Daniel 8:16 and Daniel 9:21. The available wording identifies the name itself, but the verse text is not included here, so this entry explains the name rather than Gabriel’s specific role in either passage. It is an Old Testament name preserved in the Greek rendering of Daniel.

This adjective means “old,” describing a person or thing as old in relation to age. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs seven times, all in 3 and 4 Maccabees. Its basic role is descriptive: it identifies an old person or thing rather than naming an action or event. The surrounding wording determines exactly what is described in any particular passage.

Gotholias is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 2 Kings 11:2 and once in 2 Chronicles 22:11. The name is rendered as Gotholia in the cited English translation. Its meaning here is therefore its role as a personal name; the specific person and significance in each passage require the surrounding verse text.

This word means “demon,” referring to a spiritual being associated with false worship or desolate places in the Greek Old Testament. It is a noun, so it names such a being rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from Deuteronomy, Psalms, Isaiah, and Baruch. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way that passage speaks about demons.

This word means “tree,” referring to a woody plant. It is a noun used for an individual tree or for trees generally, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 31 times, showing regular use for ordinary trees in descriptions of places, landscapes, and living things. Its basic meaning remains simple and concrete: a tree. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to one tree or more than one, but the word itself does not carry a more specialized meaning in the information available here.

This Greek LXX noun refers to something being pointed out, made known, or brought into clear view—a manifestation. It describes the disclosure or showing of something so that it can be recognized. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus, Leviticus, Psalms, and Daniel. Its use covers both an outward showing and the making known of what was previously hidden or unclear. The precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains clear: something is being revealed or openly displayed.

This noun means “through-cut; canal”: a physical passage or channel made by cutting through something. It refers to a constructed or opened route rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Exodus, Jeremiah, and Zephaniah. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a cut-through or canal.

This adjective means “double,” describing something that is twofold or present in two parts. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures, it occurs eight times, including passages in Genesis, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its use can describe a doubled amount or a paired quality, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words. It is a straightforward descriptive term rather than a name or action.

This adjective describes someone or something as “most miserable”—in an extreme state of distress, unhappiness, or wretchedness. It serves as a strong description rather than naming an action or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:4. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: it marks an especially pitiable or unhappy condition.

Ebelcharmin, also rendered Evelkharmin, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available information does not establish which kind of named entity it identifies. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Judges 11:33. Its precise significance there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Ediel, also rendered Ethil, is a proper name—the personal designation of an individual rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:36. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide a further lexical definition or explain its etymology. Its significance in that passage depends on the surrounding genealogy and verse context, which are not included here.

This noun refers to an avenger or vindicator—a person who acts to secure justice or defend someone’s cause. Its central idea is one who responds against wrong or upholds what is right. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 8:3, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word itself identifies a person by this role, rather than describing an action, event, or general quality.

gl: in the number; make up the number
d: in the number; make up the number

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something that is “in the number” or helps to “make up the number.” It points to inclusion within a counted group rather than standing outside it. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Sirach 38:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is being counted as part of a group.

This Greek LXX verb means “crumble”: to break apart or reduce something into small pieces. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Bel and the Dragon 1:33. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context, but its basic meaning remains the breaking apart of something.

This adjective describes someone as “skilful; ready”—able and prepared to act or perform well. It identifies a quality rather than an action, person, or object by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 31:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central sense is a person who is capable, competent, and prepared.

This Greek LXX verb means “unroll”: to open or spread something that has been rolled up. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at 1 Kings 7:45. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the word’s exact role in that sentence cannot be described further, but its basic meaning remains the act of unrolling or spreading out something rolled together.

This verb means “catch up” or “overtake,” describing reaching someone or something ahead and passing or drawing level with it. It expresses movement toward a person or object that is in front. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Numbers 11:23. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the act of catching up to or overtaking what lies ahead.

gl: cut on the surface; make an incision
d: cut on the surface; make an incision

e.t: ἐπιτέμνω is a verb meaning “cut on the surface; make an incision.” It describes cutting into or across a surface rather than naming an object or person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its ordinary sense is therefore clear, while its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek verb means to obtain something or to be successful in reaching an intended result. It describes coming into possession of what is sought, or achieving a favorable outcome. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, in Genesis and Proverbs, so its normal meaning is clear even though the available information does not include the surrounding verse text. The exact force in either passage depends on what is being obtained or accomplished there.

This adjective describes something pleasing or engaging—something that attracts favorable attention or gives delight. It expresses an appealing quality rather than an action or object by itself, so its precise force depends on the person or thing it describes in the sentence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 14:20. The word’s central idea is thus what is agreeable, attractive, or enjoyable to those who encounter it.

Zapha is a proper name, also presented as “Zafa,” identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament text. The name itself does not provide a descriptive meaning such as an action, quality, or role; it functions as a personal designation. This LXX word occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:16. Without the verse text, the surrounding passage is needed to determine which person the name identifies there.

This word means “already”. It is an adverb that marks something as having happened, being true, or being in place before the moment under discussion. It points to an earlier stage that has now been reached, helping readers recognize timing or prior completion. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 52 times, including passages from Genesis, Job, and Ecclesiastes. Its exact force in a sentence depends on the surrounding words and context.

Ηναδαδ is a proper name, rendered “Ēnadad” or “Inathath.” It identifies a named individual in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Ezra and three times in Nehemiah. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its specific family, role, or activity cannot be stated from the name alone.

This word means “female.” It is an adjective that identifies a person or animal as female, marking the feminine sex rather than naming a particular individual. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used in passages concerning humans, animals, and sacrificial animals, where distinguishing female from male matters. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek LXX corpus, with most occurrences in the Old Testament and one in the deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the noun or creature it describes.

Iazia is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly the person’s name rather than a general concept. This name occurs twice in the Greek text of Ezra, in Ezra 10:15 and Ezra 10:25. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain each person’s specific role in those passages.

Ieth is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name rather than as a word describing an action, quality, object, or idea. The name occurs five times in the Greek LXX, across four verses: four occurrences are in 1 Chronicles and one is in 2 Chronicles. The available information identifies the name itself, but does not provide an additional lexical definition or explain the individual’s role in each passage.

This word refers to religious service or worship offered in connection with devotion to God. As a noun, it names the act or practice of carrying out such sacred service rather than describing a person or a specific ritual by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 3:20. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine how the word functions in that particular passage, but its central meaning remains the performance of worshipful religious service.

Iram is a proper name identifying an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a descriptive word or action, but as the personal name “Iram.” This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Nehemiah 10:6. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the name alone does not establish further details about the person or the role associated with him.

Iōachal, also rendered Ioakhal, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament text represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah: once at Jeremiah 44:3 and once at Jeremiah 45:1. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily its identifying function: it designates someone named Iōachal or Ioakhal. The surrounding verse text is needed to say more about the person or each occurrence.

This noun refers to “male temple prostitutes,” describing men associated with sexual prostitution in a temple setting. It is a specific term rather than a general word for men or for prostitution. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 23:7. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context, but its basic meaning identifies these male religiously associated prostitutes.

gl: with beautiful children; blessed with fair children
d: with beautiful children; blessed with fair children

e.t: This noun describes someone “with beautiful children” or “blessed with fair children.” It expresses the favorable condition of having children regarded as beautiful or fair, rather than naming the children themselves. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 16:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning is a person characterized by having notably beautiful children.

Kanthan is a proper name, identifying a specific named entity rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:28. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not identify whether Kanthan refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the way the name functions in that verse.

Kariathiarim is a proper name used to identify a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object in general. It is rendered as “Kariathiarim” and appears 12 times across 11 Old Testament verses in the LXX corpus. Because it functions as a name, its basic meaning is identification: it points readers to the particular person, place, or entity intended in each passage, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific context.

This Greek LXX verb means “fall down.” It describes the act of moving from an upright or higher position to the ground or a lower place. The word appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, so its basic sense is consistent across several kinds of passages. It is used of people or things that descend or collapse, while the surrounding verse determines the specific situation. Its direct meaning remains physical movement downward rather than a broader idea added apart from context.

This Greek LXX verb means “appear”: it describes something becoming visible or coming into view. Its basic idea concerns manifestation rather than a person’s interpretation or response. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 48:17. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s exact force in that sentence must be determined from its immediate context rather than inferred from the word alone.

This Greek LXX noun means a “jug” or “jar”—a container used to hold and carry something. Its basic sense is an ordinary vessel, not an action or description of a person. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in 1 Kings: three times in chapter 17 and once in chapter 19. The surrounding verse determines what the container holds and how it functions in the scene, but the word itself identifies the vessel.

This word means “bin,” referring to a container used to hold something. It is a noun, so it names a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Haggai 2:16. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while the precise significance of the container in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its discussion of what is stored or measured there.

This noun refers to a swaggerer—an arrogant person who presents himself proudly and boastfully. It describes a person marked by self-important behavior rather than humility. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 20:7; the reference identifies where it appears, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its particular force there. Its basic sense remains a person whose manner is boastful, overconfident, or contemptuously self-assured.

This Greek LXX verb means “smooth,” describing the action of making something even or smooth. It is an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word appears two times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, once in 2 Samuel 22:43 and once in Psalms 17:43. Its precise object and force in either verse depend on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the making or treatment of something as smooth.

This noun means “linen” or “wick.” It refers to a tangible material, either linen used as cloth or a wick used to carry a flame. The surrounding sentence determines which sense is intended. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times in six verses, appearing in Exodus, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, and Isaiah. Its central idea is a physical fiber or strand, whether associated with clothing and fabric or with burning and light.

Maasai, also rendered Maase, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 24:18. Because the available information gives the name and reference but not the verse text or surrounding passage, its particular role there cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name Maasai or Maase.

This verb means to count or regard someone as blessed or prosperous. It describes the act of declaring that a person enjoys a favorable, flourishing condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 23 times across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it expresses a recurring way of speaking about people considered especially favored or well-off. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Mapha, also rendered Mafa, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears once, in Joshua 21:37, and identifies a named place or person in that passage. The available lexical information establishes the name’s form and rendering, but not a separate symbolic or descriptive meaning. Its precise reference in Joshua depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word means “might,” referring to the strength or capability to act. It is a noun, so it names this quality rather than describing an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wording, but its basic sense remains a reference to might or strength.

This Greek LXX particle means “actually.” It adds emphasis to a statement, drawing attention to what is truly the case rather than merely assumed or expected. As a particle, it works within a sentence to qualify or reinforce the speaker’s point, rather than naming a person, action, or object. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, all in Proverbs. That distribution indicates a compact word with a focused use, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what it emphasizes.

Meribaal is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It may also be written “Merivaal.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both within 1 Chronicles 8:34. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, this cached meaning identifies the person’s name but does not describe his family connection or role in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “remember”: to keep someone or something in mind rather than forget it. It can describe recalling the past, keeping God’s acts and commands before the mind, or calling something to mind in speech and action. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, so its basic sense is consistent across several kinds of passages. The surrounding verse determines what person, event, promise, or command is being remembered.

This noun means “beast of prey,” referring to a creature that hunts or feeds on other animals. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament represented by the Septuagint, both times in Proverbs. The word is found in Proverbs 6:6 and Proverbs 30:25, but the verse text and surrounding context are needed to explain its particular use in either passage. Its basic sense remains a predatory animal rather than a person, action, or abstract quality.

Namessi is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, in four verses: once in 1 Kings, twice in 2 Kings, and once in 2 Chronicles. Its precise reference in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but the word itself functions as a personal name.

This Greek LXX noun means “fare,” referring to the payment required for travel. It names the cost a person pays to board or use transportation, rather than the journey itself or the vehicle. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Jonah 1:3. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary meaning remains the price paid for passage. In everyday terms, it is a travel charge or paid passage.

This verb means “entertain strangers; maintain mercenary troops.” It describes providing for outsiders, whether by showing hospitality to unfamiliar people or by supporting soldiers hired for service. Thus, its central idea is supplying care or support to those who are not part of one’s own household or community. The word occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 10:14; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. This Greek LXX noun means “linen cloth,” referring to fabric made from flax. It names a material rather than an action, feeling, or person. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here: once in Judges and twice in Hosea. Its use remains concrete and ordinary, identifying linen fabric in the passages where it appears. The precise significance of the material in any one verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “howl”: to cry out with a loud, howling voice. It describes an audible action rather than a person, place, or object. The word occurs 21 times in 19 Old Testament verses within the Greek LXX corpus, with many occurrences in Isaiah and additional uses in Jeremiah, Zechariah, Amos, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a loud howl or cry.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “extremity” or “limit,” referring to an outer boundary, endpoint, or farthest extent. It can describe where something ends or the furthest point reached. The word occurs 46 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented in this corpus, so its basic idea is used across several settings rather than belonging to one isolated passage. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what boundary, endpoint, or extent the surrounding text describes.

This adverb means “overflowingly” or “extravagantly,” describing something done in an abundant, excessive, or unusually great way. It modifies an action or description by showing that it goes beyond what is ordinary, rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice: once in Psalms and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is abundance beyond the normal measure.

This verb means “refresh” or “cherish”: it describes an action that renews, revives, or lovingly cares for someone. Its basic sense is active and personal, pointing to beneficial care rather than merely observing or describing a person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 30:7. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the exact force of the action in that passage must be understood from its context.

This adjective means “of many days.” It describes a person, thing, or period in relation to a large number of days, emphasizing duration or an extended span rather than a single day or brief moment. In the LXX, it occurs four times, all within Old Testament verses, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise reference depends on the noun or situation it describes in each passage. It is not itself a verb or command; it adds a time-related quality to another word.

This is a proper name rendered “Sabai” or “Save.” It functions as a personal or place name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 6:19. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to identify precisely whom or what it names in that passage.

Samma is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. As a personal name, its meaning in a sentence is the individual who bears that name. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs twice, in 2 Samuel 23:33 and 1 Chronicles 11:44. The available information establishes the name’s identity and usage, but does not provide a separate descriptive definition or explain the surrounding verse context.

This LXX word is a proper name, rendered as “Sarad” or “Sarath.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 23:33. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular role in that passage cannot be described further, but its basic lexical function is clear: it is a personal name preserved in the Greek rendering of the Old Testament.

Saphphōth is a proper name, also given as Saffoth. It identifies a person or named figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice: once in 2 Samuel and once in Jeremiah.
